claim: The IB-to-rank conversion used in Australia is a single national schedule agreed by all the state and territory tertiary admissions centres, re-determined each February, and it is used for tertiary entrance in every Australian jurisdiction.
excerpt: This document has been prepared by the Australasian Conference of Tertiary Admissions Centres (ACTAC) to explain the procedures used by tertiary admissions centres in Australia to determine tertiary entrance rankings for students who have completed the Diploma of the International Baccalaureate. [...] The combined rank table is determined annually (in February), and is based on: the IB population weightings of the year prior to the current year as provided by the IB Development Manager - Australasia, with NT and SA treated as a single entity; the latest rank table from each of NSW, SA, Victoria, and from 2016 onwards, Queensland, with the contribution for each state weighted according to the size of its IB candidature. [...] The combined rank table is used to convert IB Diploma scores to tertiary entrance ranks for all jurisdictions in Australia.
interpretation: This is the sentence that decides how Australia is modelled here. Admission to an Australian university is run state by state - five tertiary admissions centres, each with its own rules about who may use it - but the IB conversion is not. One table, agreed nationally, applies everywhere. So the number a student carries is portable across the whole country even though the application is not, and the division between jurisdictions is a division in how you apply rather than in how you are scored. The document is from 2019 and explains the method, not the current values; the values live on UAC's page and are re-set annually.

claim: The Combined Rank is a national conversion, so an IB student can apply in any Australian state or territory and be compared with local applicants on the same scale as the ATAR.
excerpt: Results from the IB Diploma, which are reported on a whole number scale between 24 and 45, are converted into an ATAR-like value to allow IB students to be considered for tertiary places alongside their counterparts who have completed state curricula. This means that IB students can apply in any Australian state or territory with confidence about how their results compare to their peers who have completed state curricula and received an ATAR. [...] The IB Admissions Score adds more detail within each level of diploma scores but does not change the score. The IB Admissions Score will always start with the same number as your IB diploma score.
interpretation: Useful mainly for what it lets a student stop worrying about. Australian degree pages quote an entry requirement as a rank - 'lowest selection rank 90' - and a student reading that from Denmark has no way to know whether that rank means the same thing in Perth as in Sydney. It does. The corollary is that the rank is the currency and the IB score is not: a university publishing a selection rank of 90 is asking for roughly an IB 34 on the current schedule, and neither number appears on the other's page.

claim: An international applicant through UAC receives a conditional offer about 48 hours after submitting, which can be used for pre-visa assessment but does not permit enrolment; an unconditional offer, which requires results, is needed to enrol.
excerpt: International undergraduate applicants. Conditional offers: You will receive a conditional offer approximately 48 hours after you have successfully submitted your application. You may use this as part of your pre-visa assessment if required. It does not make you eligible to enrol in a course of study. To enrol, you need an unconditional offer. Unconditional offers: This table shows the UAC dates by which you need to apply and pay, and change your course preferences, to be considered for an unconditional offer in each offer round.
interpretation: This is Australia's answer to the July problem, and it is a better answer than most of Europe's. The conditional offer arrives within two days of applying, on predicted grades, and it is explicitly usable for the visa - which matters because the subclass 500 application cannot begin until the university issues a Confirmation of Enrolment, and that queue is long. The unconditional offer waits for results. Note what the two-stage structure does not do: it does not move the closing date. The application still has to be in before the cycle closes.

interpretation: The whole UAC calendar is built around the November IB session - its own key-dates sheet has IB results released from Cardiff on 17 December and IB Admissions Scores emailed the next day, which slots neatly into the December and January offer rounds. The practical reading is that a Danish candidate should expect to be admitted on predicted grades with the result confirmed later, rather than to be considered in a named round. claim: The Student visa (subclass 500) costs from AUD 2,500, requires a valid Confirmation of Enrolment in a CRICOS-registered course held at the time the visa is decided, requires Overseas Student Health Cover, allows work up to 48 hours a fortnight while the course is in session, permits a stay of up to six years in line with enrolment, and requires evidence of AUD 29,710 of living costs for twelve months plus the first twelve months of course fees and about AUD 2,000 of travel costs.
excerpt: Stay: Up to 6 years and in line with your enrolment. Cost: From AUD2,500.00 (concessions apply in limited circumstances). [...] work up to 48 hours a fortnight when your course of study or training is in session. [...] You must apply online in or outside Australia, be enrolled in a course of study in Australia and hold a valid Confirmation of Enrolment (CoE) when we decide your visa, hold Overseas Student Health Cover (OSHC), or fall in one of the exemption categories. [...] You must be enrolled in a full time course registered on the Commonwealth Register of Institutions and courses for Overseas Students (CRICOS). [...] Living costs 12-month living costs are for: students - AUD29,710 [...] Course fees: Use the first 12 months of your course fees. [...] AUD2,000 for travel costs if you are applying from anywhere else outside Australia. [...] Alternatively, you can give evidence that your parents or your partner had a personal annual income of at least AUD87,856 in the 12 months before you apply. [...] Applications lodged on or after 14 November 2025 are processed according to Ministerial Direction 115.
interpretation: The money is the part students underestimate and the sequencing is the part that catches them. There is no date to miss: the visa cannot be applied for until the university issues a Confirmation of Enrolment, and the CoE has to still be valid on the day the visa is decided, so the clock is set by the offer and by Home Affairs' queue rather than by any published deadline. That queue is not first-come-first-served either - offshore applications are ordered by a Ministerial Direction, currently Direction 115 for anything lodged from 14 November 2025. The financial test is cumulative and is not the living-cost figure alone: AUD 29,710 for twelve months of living, plus the first twelve months of tuition, plus about AUD 2,000 of travel from Europe. The alternative to showing savings is a parent's or partner's documented annual income of at least AUD 87,856, evidenced by official tax documents rather than bank statements. CRICOS registration is the quiet one: a course that is not on the register cannot carry a student visa at all, whatever else it is.

notes: Every figure on this page is indexed and moves, usually on 1 July. Re-check before quoting any of it to a student.
